```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)

orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv")
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")

orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days)) |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(
      delivery_days <= estimated_days,
      "On Time",
      "Late"
    )
  )

supply_chain_data <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(order_items, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  mutate(
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price
  )
```

This exploration examines how seller scale, delivery performance, freight cost, and product characteristics interact across the marketplace.

The goal is to identify which seller groups are helping the marketplace grow efficiently and which groups may require more operational attention.

**Business question:** Which seller segments are helping the marketplace scale efficiently, and which ones are creating high fulfillment costs or weak operational performance?

## Marketplace benchmark

Before comparing seller groups, I first calculated overall marketplace performance.

```{r}
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance
```

The marketplace contains **`r overall_performance$total_items` item rows**.

Average delivery time is **`r round(overall_performance$average_delivery_days, 1)` days**, average freight cost is **`r round(overall_performance$average_freight_cost, 1)`**, and the overall on-time delivery rate is **`r round(overall_performance$on_time_rate, 1)`%**.

These values provide the benchmark for the rest of the analysis.

```{r}
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100
```

## 1. Scale and reliability

The first question is whether the seller groups handling the most marketplace activity are also delivering reliably.

### 1.a Seller scale and reliability

This chart shows which seller states matter most by volume, while also labeling their on-time delivery rates.

```{r}
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = reorder(seller_name, total_items),
    y = total_items,
    fill = on_time_rate
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(on_time_rate, 1), "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#8ecae6",
    high = "#023047"
  ) +
  expand_limits(y = max(top_8_states$total_items) * 1.12) +
  labs(
    title = "The largest seller groups do not all perform equally well",
    subtitle = "Bar length shows item volume; labels show on-time delivery performance",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Number of Items",
    fill = "On-Time Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r largest_state$seller_name`** handles **`r largest_state$total_items` items**, representing about **`r round(largest_state_share, 1)`%** of marketplace activity.

This means seller scale matters, but scale alone is not enough. A seller group is more attractive when that volume is combined with strong delivery performance.

### 1.b Above or below the benchmark

I next compared each major seller state directly with the overall marketplace on-time delivery rate.

```{r}
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = difference_from_average > 0),
    size = 4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Difference from the overall marketplace on-time rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Above Average"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r best_delivery_state$seller_name`** performs strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while **`r weakest_delivery_state$seller_name`** performs weakest among the eight largest seller states.

## 2. Operational pressure

Delivery performance and freight burden should not be judged separately.

A seller group with strong delivery and low freight burden is in a different position from one with weak delivery and high shipping burden.

```{r}
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = average_freight_ratio,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = total_items,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = overall_performance$average_freight_ratio,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Some seller groups face pressure from both cost and delivery performance",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents marketplace item volume",
    x = "Average Freight-to-Price Ratio",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** Seller groups below the delivery benchmark and above the freight benchmark deserve the closest operational attention, especially when they also handle a large number of items.

## 3. Marketplace activity over time

Seller performance should also be interpreted through time.

A marketplace can behave differently when activity rises, so I summarized item volume by month and year.

```{r}
monthly_activity <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(purchase_year, purchase_month) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

peak_month <- monthly_activity |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)
```

### 3.a Activity trend across the year

```{r}
ggplot(
  monthly_activity,
  aes(
    x = purchase_month,
    y = total_items,
    group = 1
  )
) +
  geom_area(
    fill = "#8ecae6",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#023047",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#fb8500",
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ purchase_year) +
  labs(
    title = "Marketplace activity rises and falls across the year",
    subtitle = "Area shows monthly item volume while the line highlights the trend",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** The highest-volume period occurs in month **`r peak_month$purchase_month`** of **`r peak_month$purchase_year`**, with **`r peak_month$total_items` items**.

The on-time delivery rate during that period was approximately **`r round(peak_month$on_time_rate, 1)`%**.

## 4. What drives freight cost?

Higher freight cost does not automatically mean poor seller performance.

Part of the difference may simply come from the kinds of products being shipped.

### 4.a Overall weight-to-freight relationship

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

supply_chain_data |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#4361EE",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    color = "#F72585",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Heavier products generally cost more to ship",
    subtitle = "The highlighted line shows the overall relationship",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** Freight cost generally increases as product weight increases.

This tells us that some of the freight burden is driven by product mix rather than by seller inefficiency alone.

### 4.b State-level freight patterns

I then separated the four largest seller states to see whether the same pattern appears in each market.

```{r}
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "gray70",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = seller_name),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.6
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Minas Gerais" = "#F72585",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "São Paulo" = "#7209B7"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The freight trend changes across major seller states",
    subtitle = "Each colored line highlights the weight-to-freight relationship within one state",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** All four major seller states show a positive relationship between product weight and freight cost, but the strength of that pattern is not identical across states.

Using separate colored lines makes those differences easier to see.

## 5. Freight cost variation

Average freight cost can hide unusually expensive shipments.

To look beyond the average, I compared the freight-cost distributions of the five largest seller states.

```{r}
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides large differences between shipments",
    subtitle = "Freight-cost distributions for the five largest seller states",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r highest_freight_state$seller_name`** has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states at approximately **`r round(highest_freight_state$average_freight_cost, 1)`**.

The distribution also shows that some seller states contain much more spread in freight cost than others.

## 6. Management takeaway

The exploration shows that seller performance should not be judged using volume, delivery performance, or freight cost alone.

High-volume seller groups matter because even small changes can affect a large number of marketplace items.

Higher freight cost should also not automatically be treated as seller inefficiency because heavier products naturally cost more to ship.

Management should pay the closest attention to seller groups that combine:

- high marketplace volume,
- delivery performance below the benchmark,
- freight burden above the benchmark,
- large freight-cost variation, and
- freight costs that cannot be fully explained by heavier products.
